name: user_contacts
description: Email and phone contacts of a user. The login email is the row referenced by users.email_id.

columns.name: email_verification_code
columns.description: Secret. Never logged, never returned in a response.
columns.note: Legacy draws 64 random bits into a MariaDB `bigint unsigned`. Neither target database has that column: PostgreSQL `bigint` and SQLite `INTEGER` are both signed 64 bit, so the top bit is already gone. The bound is set lower still, at 2^53-1, because SQLite hands an INTEGER to JavaScript as a double — a wider value would come back changed on the reference path without anything failing. 53 bits is 9.0e15 codes against a window of a few hours; the entropy is not what is scarce here.

columns.name: email_opt_in_type_id
columns.note: Not an identifier despite the name — it holds an OptInType value.

notes: email is globally unique, unlike users.gradido_id which is unique per community. Two communities cannot share an email address.

updated_at is maintained by the database in legacy (ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP). PostgreSQL needs a trigger and SQLite needs the application to set it — so the fast path and the reference path must both write it explicitly rather than rely on the dialect.
created_at, updated_at and deleted_at are UTC milliseconds; see types/Timestamp.json.

Identifiers are uint64 throughout. Legacy is inconsistent here — users.id is int unsigned while referrer_id, contribution_link_id and publisher_id, which point at it, are bigint unsigned. A foreign key narrower than its target truncates silently in C, so gradido2 uses one width everywhere.
